canberra.title: Activist wanted to ‘send a message about peace’ by trespassing at weapons facility
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This story references allegations of sexual assault. A human rights activist has declared she’ll keep “bangi...
canberra.content:
6 August 2026

Juliet Lamont, 55, standing outside court with supporters following her sentencing. Photo: Claire Sams.

CONTENT WARNING: This story references allegations of sexual assault.

A human rights activist has declared she’ll keep “banging the drum” of justice after escaping a conviction for trespassing on the site of a weapons manufacturer.

On 21 July 2025, Juliet Lamont from the NSW Northern Rivers region went to a facility owned by Electro Optic Systems (EOS) in Symonston with a group of activists.

They climbed the facility’s roof and remained there for several hours, holding protest signs, before police removed them.

The ACT Magistrates Court heard the 55-year-old was one of eight people charged over the incident. She formally pleaded guilty to a trespass charge on Tuesday (4 August).

Her lawyer, Bernard Collaery, said Lamont chose to trespass after the weapons company exhibited at an event in southern Israel, but said the activists had been unable to prove that the “armaments [were] travelling to Israel through intermediaries”.

He said she became a peace activist because she “opposes all forms of violence” and asked the court not to convict her.

“I’ve dealt with protesters on both sides of the issue … the thing that I look for in criminal records is vandalism and threats to public safety – neither of which are present in this woman’s record,” he said.

The prosecutor said that Lamont appeared to have “a bit more involvement” than her fellow activists in the incident and described her criminal history as showing a “pattern” of behaviour.

He also pointed to “some fear and some distress” among EOS employees, saying that while the protest was non-violent, they didn’t know that at the time.

“They have the right to demonstrate, but they need to do things lawfully. They don’t have the right to break the law,” he said of the group.

Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson discharged the trespass charge without recording a conviction against her.

She said Lamont went to the facility to “send a message about peace” and described her as otherwise being of “very good character”.

“I do find that the offence was committed under extenuating circumstances because you do hold a deep conviction … You have taken huge personal risks to address that, probably the least of which was getting on the roof of the EOS building.”

She also handed Lamont a six-month recognisance order, with a $5 surety.

Speaking outside court after her sentencing, Lamont told the media that she believed the outcome showed that her actions were on the “right side of history”.

“I think she realised that everything I do is to bring awareness to the genocide in Palestine, and I think my sentence reflected that,” she said of the decision.

Lamont also travelled to Gaza on a humanitarian flotilla before being intercepted by Israeli forces.

She alleged flotilla members endured sexual assault and torture during their detention, and said she hoped to give evidence about the allegations before the International Criminal Court.

Lamont said she wasn’t deterred by the trespass charge being brought against her, noting she planned to take a leadership role in activism in the future.

canberra.title: Public Sector Standards Commissioner should probe CIT CEO’s conduct, says privileges committee
canberra.snippet: The Public Sector Standards Commissioner should investigate whether the conduct of embattled CIT CEO Margot McNeill before Legislative As...
canberra.content:
CIT CEO Dr Margot McNeill was found to be uncooperative and possibly obstructive. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The Public Sector Standards Commissioner should investigate whether the conduct of embattled CIT CEO Margot McNeill before Legislative Assembly committees breached public sector values and undermined the integrity and reputation of the public service, a Legislative Assembly privileges committee has recommended.

The Select Privileges Committee formed to inquire into Dr McNeill’s possible contempt of the Public Administration and Accounts Committee, which inquired into her recruitment, was unable to determine whether she was in contempt of the Legislative Assembly due to her continued refusal to cooperate.

It found that Dr McNeill’s overly litigious and combative approach to the committee’s inquiries raised concerns about whether her conduct was inconsistent with public sector values and undermined the integrity and reputation of the service, contrary to section 9 of the Public Sector Management Act 1994.

It said that if necessary, the CIT Board should refer Dr McNeill to the commissioner.

The report said that senior public officials should engage in a way that discharges their duties under the Act and the Public Sector Code of Conduct.

It said that Dr McNeill would be expected to represent CIT before Assembly Committees during Estimates and Annual Reports hearings at a minimum.

“The way in which these events have undermined committee members’ confidence in Dr McNeill’s possible responses should be a concern for CIT and the ACTPS as institutions,” the report said.

The committee’s findings have only strengthened calls from independent MLA Thomas Emerson for the CIT Board to dismiss the CEO, who remains on leave with no return date.

Mr Emerson said Dr McNeill was on paid leave at a cost to taxpayers of almost $8500 per week while the organisation she led was rolling out voluntary redundancies.

“Four weeks ago, I wrote to the CIT board chair outlining serious concerns with Dr McNeill’s ongoing tenure as CEO of CIT. This Privileges Committee report only strengthens these concerns,” he said.

“Dr McNeill has been afforded every opportunity to clear the air, and yet another committee process has been obstructed by her refusal to do so.

“Due process is important, but so too is the appropriate use of public funds and the integrity of our public institutions.”

Mr Emerson said it was unfair on all the hard-working staff trying to deliver a quality student experience at CIT to have their work undermined by repeated and ongoing trainwrecks at the executive level.

The contempt inquiry stemmed from a TAFE NSW media statement that contradicted Dr McNeill’s assertion during the first committee hearing that her former employer had instructed her not to disclose that she was under investigation for serious misconduct during her CIT recruitment or the subsequent finding against her when she was three months into her CEO role.

The privileges committee took issue with Dr McNeill’s refusal to provide any documented evidence to support her assertion that she was acting on legal advice, her reliance on lawyers during both inquiries and her insistent and unsupported claims of legal professional privilege over that legal advice.

“Dr McNeill continued to rely heavily on legal representation during this inquiry, and it resulted in the overly legalistic approach that the PAA committee raised concerns about,” the committee’s report said.

“Tiresome and unwarranted attempts to instruct and threaten this committee about its powers and scope of inquiry were neither helpful nor welcome.

“The assertion of legal professional privilege over apparently non-existent documents was also fundamentally unhelpful and could be perceived as an attempt to mislead, distract, and obstruct the committee’s attempts to seek further information and documents to assist with its inquiry.”

Her claim of legal professional privilege in a lawyer’s letter dated 12 June 2026 is confusing at best, and deliberately obstructive at worst.

TAFE NSW, citing ongoing legal action by Dr McNeill, refused to provide any information that could verify its media statement or corroborate or refute her evidence to the PAA Committee.

“In the absence of this information, this committee is unable to test whether the statements concerned were misleading or not, and therefore, whether it amounts to contempt of the Assembly pursuant to standing order 277,” the report said.

The committee did find Dr McNeill’s refusal to answer questions about whether she supplied fresh documents to the media supporting her position after the PAA committee report was published contemptuous in the normal sense.

The initial inquiry found that Dr McNeill actively misled the CIT board by denying that TAFE NSW had found her to be in breach of her employment contract.

It was launched after it became public that Dr McNeill had failed to disclose that she was the subject of an investigation into allegations of misconduct during her recruitment, allegations that were substantiated.

The committee found that Dr McNeill should have disclosed to the CIT board that TAFE NSW was investigating her conduct before accepting the appointment at CIT in May 2025.

canberra.title: Independent AUKUS public inquiry hearings coming to east coast
canberra.snippet: Hearings into Australia’s participation in AUKUS are set to resume next week on Australia’s east coast after a series of hearings was hel...
canberra.content:
Inquiry commissioners Leanne Minshull, Admiral Chris Barrie (Ret’d), Peter Garrett, and Karina Lester at the Canberra launch of the inquiry in June. Photo: Screenshot.

Hearings into Australia’s participation in AUKUS are set to resume next week on Australia’s east coast after a series of hearings was held in southern and western states.

The independent Public Inquiry into AUKUS was established in June to look into Australia’s commitment to buy nuclear-powered submarines under the AUKUS Pillar I construct with the US and UK.

The inquiry is being led by former Labor minister and Midnight Oil frontman Peter Garrett, and includes fellow commissioners former WA Labor premier and federal Labor minister Dr Carmen Lawrence, former Chief of Navy and Chief of Defence Force Admiral Chris Barrie (Ret’d), the co-CEO of the Australia Institute Leanne Minshull, and Yankunytjatjara woman Karina Lester.

An initiative of the Australian Peace and Security Forum, the inquiry is being partly crowdfunded, but also has the support of a number of organisations including the Independent and Peaceful Australia Network, the Australian Conservation Foundation, ICAN Australia, the Sydney Peace Foundation, and Australians for War Powers Reform.

Support for the inquiry has also come from several labour organisations including the Maritime Union of Australia, the Electrical Trades Union, the Australian Education Union, and the South Coast Labour Council.

After an initial introductory hearing in Canberra on 3 June, the inquiry moved to Melbourne on 11 June, Fremantle on 29 June, and Adelaide on 16 July. A virtual Q&A was also held on 3 August.

On Monday (10 August) the inquiry will move to NSW Parliament House on Macquarie Street in Sydney, and will be followed by a hearing at Newcastle City Hall at 290 King Street in Newcastle on Tuesday.

The BlueScope Gallery in Wollongong will host a hearing on Wednesday, and then a two-day event will be held on Wednesday 2 and Thursday 3 September at the Australian Centre for Christianity and Culture (ACCC) at 15 Blackall St in Barton, ACT.

The inquiry has so far heard from prominent Australians, many with informed insights into the AUKUS Pillar I construct which plans to see Australia acquire between three and five Virginia-class nuclear-powered submarines from the US from 2032, and then up to eight SSN-AUKUS-class nuclear-powered submarines to be built at Osborne in Adelaide for delivery in the 2040s.

Debate has centred around whether Australia needs nuclear-powered submarines at a projected cost of $368 billion, compared to the much cheaper option of conventional diesel-electric powered boats.

There is also concern in east and west coast communities about the basing locations of nuclear-powered submarines – particularly in the Illawarra – as well as where nuclear waste will be stored.

“Both Wollongong/Port Kembla and Newcastle are in the frame for hosting submarine bases for AUKUS,” Mr Garrett said in a statement.

“As we heard from former Defence Minister Linda Reynolds at the Perth hearings, this will likely make these great cities future military targets. We encourage citizens in all three cities to register to attend the hearings and hear the evidence for themselves.”

The inquiry is taking submissions from the public and subject matter experts and, to date, more than 500 written submissions have been received.

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: Man refused bail over alleged assault of ‘vulnerable’ victim
canberra.snippet: CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to an allegation of rape. A man has failed in his bid for freedom after being accused of assaulting a ...
canberra.content:
6 August 2026

The man wanted to be released to live in regional NSW. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

CONTENT WARNING: This story refers to an allegation of rape.

A man has failed in his bid for freedom after being accused of assaulting a “vulnerable victim”.

In the ACT Magistrates Court on Wednesday (5 August), his defence lawyer sought the man’s release on bail.

Region has chosen not to name the accused man on this occasion to avoid identifying the alleged victim, as the relationship between the two wasn’t immediately clear.

He has been charged with one count of sexual intercourse without consent.

His lawyer said his client would be “vulnerable” in custody due to his mental health diagnoses, and suggested he stay with his ill mother in a NSW Central West town upon release.

“It’ll take at least 12 months for this matter to proceed to a trial,” he said.

“Your Honour, the bail concerns that the prosecution have outlined [can be ameliorated by having him] residing with his mum.”

The prosecutor, who opposed bail, alleged the man carried out a “violent assault” over several days in July.

He urged the court to refuse bail on the risk the man could interfere with witnesses or evidence.

“The offender has shown, consistently, a pattern of violent offending and a disregard for court orders,” he said.

Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson ultimately refused the man’s bid for freedom and said the allegations indicated he posed an “unjustifiable risk” to the community.

She said there was an “extremely high” risk of him interfering with witnesses or evidence, or offending on release, if bail was granted.

“[He is] alleged to have commenced a five-day assault on a vulnerable victim,” she said.

She also said the man’s criminal history was “littered with examples” of his contravening court orders across several states, which raised a “very grave risk” that he would not follow his bail conditions if released.

Special Magistrate Wilson said that while the man wanted to be released on bail to live interstate, some of his criminal history was recorded in that town.

The man will next face court in September.

australia.title: Texts suggest Angus Taylor ‘paid money to the Reformers … or was refusing to’, Icac inquiry hears
australia.snippet: Jean-Claude Perrottet, brother of former NSW premier, asked about messages referencing federal opposition leader and factional group Refo...
australia.content:
New South Wales’ anti-corruption watchdog has been shown text messages which suggest Angus Taylor “had paid some money to the Reformers … or was refusing to”, according to the lawyer assisting the inquiry.

Taylor, the federal opposition leader, is not named in Icac’s allegations and has previously denied making payments to the hard-right factional group the Reformers.

Jean-Claude Perrottet, a member, was on Thursday read text messages sent by Reformer cofounder Christian Ellis in September 2021. Ellis says the group has “zero dollars at the moment” in one message.

Jean-Claude asks why and Ellis replies: “Because Michael O’Hara hates the vax campaign, and Angus Taylor hates Rob.”

The counsel assisting Icac, Juliet Curtin, asked: “That seems to be suggesting that Mr Taylor had paid some money to the Reformers too, doesn’t it, or was refusing to?”

Jean-Claude replied: “It sounds like that’s the suggestion.” Curtin then said: “Do you know anything about that?”

“Look, I’ve heard it come up [at the inquiry], but until that came up, I hadn’t recalled that at all,” the younger brother of the former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet said.

Dominic Perrottet is not named in Icac’s allegations and is not accused of wrongdoing.

The inquiry has previously heard evidence, including from Reformers cofounder Robert Assaf, that hotelier Michael O’Hara threatened to end an arrangement in which he paid lobbying company Beckington for Reformers factional work after the group adopted an anti-vaccination stance.

Inquiry hears intercepted calls

Late on Thursday, the inquiry heard intercepted phone calls from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif for the first time since the opening day of the inquiry.

The corruption watchdog is examining an allegation that between 2020 and 2023, Nassif and his company Toplace made prohibited donations solicited or accepted by Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Nassif.

They including the damage to the career of former Liberal minister and Baulkham Hills MP David Elliott and the removal of the then building commissioner David Chandler, but the inquiry has yet to focus extensively on the allegation.

On Thursday afternoon, Jean-Claude Perrottet was played three phone calls between him and Nassif in 2021, when he was managing shares for Nassif while working at Medallion Financial.

In one call, Nassif can be heard asking Jean-Claude Perrottet to withdraw “100” from his portfolio to give to “to your brother, to Jeremy or Chris” for “preselection”.

Asked about which brother Nassif was proposing to give $100,000, Jean-Claude Perrottet said he didn’t know.

“I don’t know what he’s talking about, to be honest with you,” he said, rejecting the suggestion the money was to support the Reformers recruitment work, describing the call as “nonsense”.

He was played another call, previously heard on the first day of the inquiry, in which Nassif can be heard to claim that he “fucked him [David Elliott] sideways”, forcing “the boys” to get rid of the former Liberal MP’s seat of Baulkham Hills, and had sent “Castle Hill fucking hundreds of new members”.

Jean-Claude Perrottet described the call, in which he also thanked Nassif for “all the support for the family”, as “nonsensical”.

“That’s a throwaway comment that gets used all the time,” he said of his remark to Nassif about his family, saying he was not aware of Nassif providing financial support to bring new Liberal members to the Castle Hill branch.

He described a third phone call, in which Nassif complained about Chandler, who had been scrutinising his developments for defects, as “crazy talk”.

In the call, Nassif allegedly said he “had been promised that the commissioner will be fucking stopped or chased or fucking done something to him”, asking if Jean-Claude Perrottet “can take a message to Charlie or to Dom, the building commissioner, we need to stop him”, and making a subsequent request to “get Charlie to do something please”.

Under questioning, Jean-Claude Perrottet accepted that Nassif had made frequent references to his brother, Charles Perrottet, but said he had never heard of his brother agreeing to do anything for Nassif of the nature discussed.

Charles Perrottet, who has been named in Icac’s allegation, has previously denied any wrongdoing. Nassif, who fled Australia for regional Lebanon in 2022, is not expected to appear at Icac’s inquiry and has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Questions over monthly payments

Jean-Claude, earlier on Thursday, told the corruption inquiry he did not know why he received monthly payments of $5,000 from a lobbying company alleged to have accepted prohibited political donations.

The corruption watchdog is investigating whether the Reformers solicited or accepted illegal donations for the recruitment or renewal of members to the Liberal party.

That practice, known as branch stacking, is not illegal.

Curtin asked about invoices for four monthly payments of $5,000 and one payment of $5,500 from registered lobbying company Beckington between April and August 2021.

The inquiry has previously heard that Beckington, set up by Ellis and Greenwood in 2019, received payments from prohibited donor and hotelier O’Hara for factional work after issuing fake invoices for consulting advice.

Asked about the “substantial injections of cash” into his account, Jean-Claude said: “I’m honestly trying to do my best here. I honestly don’t recall why I might have done some work for them [Beckington].”

“I don’t know. I mean, it could have been for work. I mean, maybe, maybe Christian owed me money. I don’t know,” Jean-Claude told the inquiry.

The commission had previously heard Jean-Claude Perrotet travelled to Fiji to avoid summons to appear at a parliamentary inquiry in 2023 which preceded Icac’s probe.

On Thursday he told the commission: “Yes, I went to Fiji. I was not in a good place, and I didn’t want to partake in what I believed was a sham inquiry.”

The watchdog revealed its witnesses for next week, including Greenwood, who has been named in two allegations.

Last week, the inquiry heard that a screenshot of a message from Dallas McInerney, the then chief executive of Catholic Schools NSW, was sent to Reformers members in which McInerney said he planned to “shake down Angus for 10k” during a breakfast meeting with ministers.

The message was allegedly sent in March 2021 when Taylor was energy minister in the Morrison government.

Dylan Whitelaw, another Reformers associate, was read a later-intercepted text message in which he claimed McInerney had told him he had secured a commitment from Taylor for a “15k injection and a 3k monthly donation!”

Whitelaw couldn’t recall sending the message and told the inquiry he would be “very surprised” if Taylor made any contribution. McInerney, who is a factional ally of Taylor, will appear at the inquiry next week.

Contacted for comment on Thursday, Taylor’s office pointed to previous statements made by the Liberal leader: “I have already made my position clear. No payments were made. The commission has made no allegation that I engaged in any wrongdoing or unlawful conduct. It would be wrong and misleading to suggest otherwise.”

Icac’s inquiry continues.

australia.title: ‘Performative reductions’: Labor MPs and business groups urge Burke against sweeping immigration changes
australia.snippet: MPs say they are anxious for the government to avoid cuts to family and humanitarian visa categories Get our breaking news email , free a...
australia.content:
Major business groups have urged Labor to suspend its immigration changes and consult further with industry about how to get more skilled workers into the country, amid questions about looming Labor tweaks on permanent migration.

With the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, delaying an anticipated immigration speech by at least one week, some Labor MPs say they are anxious to avoid major changes to the family and humanitarian visa categories, with one urging against “performative reductions” in migration in response to One Nation.

But other Labor sources characterised Burke’s changes as tweaks to existing settings, with an expected focus on enforcement of existing rules and small pruning of various programs.

“Tony’s doing an absolutely fantastic job of ensuring, that our immigration program which is so vital for us economically, vital for our vibrancy … the world’s most successful multicultural nation. But it must be properly calibrated,” said the energy minister, Chris Bowen.

Burke was to deliver a National Press Club address on Thursday about migration policy, but withdrew on Tuesday with a spokesperson telling media “some elements of the speech would not be finalised” in time.

The ABC reported measures could include tougher family visa rules, capping backpacker numbers, or restrictions on asylum seekers. Burke’s office would not confirm media reports, and senior sources in the government remained tight-lipped on the changes.

Some sources said they believed media and stakeholder focus on Burke’s speech had been overegged, characterising the changes as more “surgical” adjustments across multiple migration areas, and downplaying major changes to work, family or humanitarian visas.

Another Labor source said they expected Burke’s speech would focus on how Labor plans to cut permanent migration to 185,000 a year – a target the government has cited in budget papers – rather than any cuts below that number.

That figure includes about 132,000 skilled migration places and 52,000 partner and family visas.

But potential cuts to either stream are already facing pushback from business groups and government members.

Outside what will be detailed in Burke’s speech, his department recently announced that skilled migrants who were already in Australia would be given priority for permanent residency, which could help lower total migrant numbers, but also decrease the pipeline of available workers.

The Minerals Council of Australia called on the government to “suspend skilled migration changes and consult industry” more closely on those changes.

The MCA chief executive, Tania Constable, said the reforms would “make it harder for mining and other sectors”, raising fears about skills shortages and risks to project timelines, earnings and the economy. She said mining companies were already struggling to find workers.

“Demand from these sectors for specialised skills is already growing faster than migration pathways can adapt, and industry is frustrated and impeded by slow updates, credential barriers and settlement constraints,” Constable said.

The acting prime minister, Richard Marles, denied rumours of a disagreement with Burke in a cabinet meeting on Monday.

“Migration obviously plays a really significant part in our economy, but it needs to happen at a sustainable rate,” he said.

Pauline Hanson told News 24 that she didn’t care if employers groups thought a migrant crackdown “is going to affect their businesses”.

“I don’t care. My concern is for those Australians that can’t get a roof over their head,” she said.

Labor MP Jerome Laxale told the ABC that Labor would strive to meet its 185,000 permanent migration target.

“If that requires tweaks to our policy to do so, we just have to do that,” he said.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive, Andrew McKellar, said it would be a “concern” if Labor was to trim working holidaymakers, while cutting family visas would also be a disincentive to attracting skilled workers.

“The government should proceed with caution, we don’t want to shoot ourselves in the foot,” he said.

“It would have a damaging impact if the government was to try to curtail those categories in a draconian way.”

Master Builders Australia chief executive, Denita Wawn, added that the datacentres boom would need a new boost to construction workers, and called for tradespeople to be prioritised.

“Migrant tradies ultimately contribute to far more homes than they consume, especially when they reside here over the long term,” Wawn said.

Guardian Australia also spoke to several Labor MPs who said the government should tread carefully around partner visas, warning any cut to family categories would raise anxiety across communities.

One MP said everyone including the government should stop being “hysterical” about migration numbers, and wanted to see firmer pushback by Labor against One Nation’s immigration rhetoric.

“I am against performative reductions, I am in favour of steady migration … Getting skilled people in from overseas is imperative,” they said.

“[Burke is] possibly driven by desire to be seen to be reducing migration rather than anything of substance.”

Another MP said they would be concerned if the government reduced Australia’s humanitarian intake, while a third said cutting backpackers could be a way forward.

One MP said there was confusion among those outside the cabinet who had not yet been advised of any changes. All said the issue was complex, and while reform across the system was needed, that the messaging was critical – especially amid the rise of Hanson and One Nation’s anti-immigration agenda raising fears in migrant communities.

australia.content:
Icac witness asked about ‘filthy schools money’ messages

Penry Buckley

Returning to the NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny, Jean-Claude Perrottet has been asked about messages read out on the first day of the inquiry.

On 12 January 2023, Reformer Jeremy Greenwood allegedly wrote to him:

Hey, so you know how I’m good to you and help you and give you all your filthy schools money … and put up with your fucking whining?

Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote back: “Don’t put that in writing.”

Greenwood replied: “It deletes.”

Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asks if the messages are “because it wasn’t money that you or he were being paid for any work that you were doing for Catholic Schools NSW?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “No, I think Jeremy was doing work for Catholic Schools.”

Curtin: “Why is he, why is he calling it filthy schools money?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “I can’t speak to his thoughts, but he’s having a crack at me.”

Curtin: “OK, well then, if it was just a joke and he’s having a crack, why do you then respond quickly: ‘Don’t put that in writing’?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Why would I want that in writing?”

Curtin: “Why wouldn’t you?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Because it’s not true.”

What we learned – Thursday 6 August

That’s where we’ll leave our live coverage for the day.

Before we log off, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • Almost 600 childcare services were shut down in the latest quarter, a twentyfold increase on the same quarter last year, as federal, state and territory governments crack down on dodgy and underperforming providers.

  • The government has asked the consumer watchdog to draw up some national safety standards to crack down on the sale of unsafe ebikes in Australia.

  • News Corp has delivered a strong rise in revenue across its global business, despite weakness in its news division, marked by a slide in digital subscribers at its Australian mastheads.

  • A 60-year-old good Samaritan has died after he was allegedly attacked by shoplifting youths outside a Melbourne shopping strip.

  • Gina Rinehart has lost an estimated $283m on paper as Elon Musk’s SpaceX company slumps in value.

  • The federal parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence directed at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people is continuing this week, with hearings held in Melbourne.

  • New South Wales’s anti-corruption watchdog has been shown text messages which suggest Angus Taylor “had paid some money to the Reformers … or was refusing to”, according to the lawyer assisting the inquiry. Taylor, the federal opposition leader, is not named in Icac’s allegations and has previously denied making payments to the rightwing factional group the Reformers.

  • The ABC has apologised to Gina Rinehart for a short film that appeared on its Race Around the World program.

  • A case of H5N1 bird flu has been confirmed in an Australian land-based bird for the first time after a magpie on Victoria’s south-west coast tested positive.

  • Locals have been urged to evacuate immediately after a fire in Port Adelaide at an industrial shed used to store sulphur began producing large volumes of toxic smoke.

Thanks for sticking around, see you tomorrow morning!

Members of Brethren church and Advance to appear at parliamentary inquiry on 2025 election

Krishani Dhanji

Members of the Plymouth Brethren Christian church and the rightwing lobby group Advance will appear at a parliamentary inquiry reviewing the 2025 federal election.

In the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters’ interim report, released last month, the committee said Australia’s democracy had come “under assault” at the last federal election from “significant third parties”.

The committee received dozens of reports about the conduct of members by the Brethren, who supported Liberal candidates in marginal seats across the country. The committee’s report made several recommendations including a new code of conduct for campaigners.

The Labor MP Jerome Laxale, chair of the committee, says the two groups have confirmed they will attend the next public hearing on 21 August as the inquiry continues:

Transparency is one of the pillars of our democracy, and voters deserve to know who is involved in campaigning at our polling booths.

I thank the Plymouth Brethren Christian Church and Advance for confirming their upcoming attendance to provide evidence to the Committee as we further consider these important issues.

Penry Buckley

Icac concludes for the day as Jean-Claude Perrottet admits to travelling to Fiji to avoid ‘sham inquiry’

Jean-Claude Perrottet has now concluded two days of evidence before Icac’s Operation Rosny. Under the final questions from counsel assisting Juliet Curtin, he was asked about whether he received a leaked confidential draft report from a 2023 parliamentary inquiry which preceded Icac’s probe.

On Wednesday, the NSW Liberal upper house member Damien Tudehope admitted leaking the report to Reformer Jeremy Greenwood, but Jean-Claude Perrottet says he does not recall the report being passed on to him. He is shown an email from Greenwood to him in February 2023 which includes the report as an attachment and the message “Do not share with anyone”, and his own response.

The inquiry has previously heard that Jean-Claude Perrottet travelled to Fiji to avoid being served a summons to appear at the inquiry. Asked about this, he says:

Yes, I went to Fiji. I was not in a good place, and I didn’t want to partake in what I believed was a sham inquiry.

Finally, following evidence by Reformer Robert Assaf earlier this week that Greenwood may have coached Jean-Claude Perrottet about the evidence he would give to Icac earlier this year, he says he may have spoken to Greenwood about Icac, “but I don’t remember Jeremy saying that”.

Penry Buckley

Icac witness says developer’s claim of promise to remove building commissioner was ‘crazy talk’

In the third phone call that Icac hears between Jean-Claude Perrottet and fugitive property developer Jean Nassif, Nassif can be heard complaining about the building commissioner David Chandler who had been scrutinising his developments for defects.

“I’ve been promised that the commissioner will be fucking stopped or chased or fucking done something to him,” says Nassif, who goes on to to describe Chandler as “the worst bulldog bully”.

In the call, Nassif asks if Jean-Claude Perrottet “can take a message to Charlie or or to Dom, the building commissioner, we need to stop him”, making a subsequent request to “get Charlie to do something please”.

Under questioning, Jean-Claude Perrottet accepts that Nassif made frequent references to his brother Charles Perrottet, but describes the call as “crazy talk”.

He has the following exchange with counsel assisting Juliet Curtin:

Curtin: “And when you say it’s crazy talk, we take from that that you were completely surprised when Mr Nassif suggested that you should convey these messages to Charles?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Yes.”

Curtin: “And you have never heard of Charles agreeing to do anything for Mr Nassif?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “No, I haven’t.”

Charles Perrottet, who has been named in Icac’s allegation, has previously denied any wrongdoing, while Dominic Perrottet is not accused of any wrongdoing.

NSW man fined $5,000 over threats to kill federal MP and family

A Sydney man has been sentenced after being found guilty of sending online threats to a federal parliamentarian.

It comes after federal authorities investigated two emails sent to the parliamentarian’s office that threatened to kill the politician and their family.

The 31-year-old was arrested after police seized electronic devices during a search of his Bankstown home in December last year.

He was sentenced to a Community Corrections Order and fined $5,000.

Man arrested after stabbing in Sydney’s west

A 38-year-old man has been arrested after an alleged stabbing outside a shopping centre in Sydney’s west.

Emergency services responded to reports of a stabbing on Thursday morning at Lalor Park, where they treated a 53-year-old man before taking him to Westmead Hospital in a serious condition.

A crime scene was established and after searching a nearby unit, NSW Police arrested a 38-year-old man.

Anyone with dashcam or mobile footage of the incident has been urged to contact Blacktown Police Station or Crime Stoppers.

Penry Buckley

Continuing from the previous post…

In a second call, played on the first day of the inquiry, Nassif can be heard to claim that he “fucked him [David Elliott] sideways”, forcing “the boys” to get rid of the former Liberal MP’s seat of Baulkham Hills, and sent “Castle Hill fucking hundreds of new members”.

In the call, in which Nassif claims to have “been speaking to your brothers every day” about Covid lockdowns, Jean-Claude Perrottet also thanks Nassif for “all the support for the family”. Today, he says the call is “nonsensical”.

Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asks:

One way that he could have sent hundreds of new members to Castle Hill was by providing financial support for those who were attempting to recruit new members to Castle Hill?

Jean-Claude Perrottet says: “Yes, he could have done that, but I’m not aware of that.”

Asked about the comment he made to Nassif about support for his family, he said:

That’s a throwaway comment that gets used all the time.

Nassif, who fled Australia for regional Lebanon in 2022, is not expected to appear at Icac’s inquiry and has previously denied any wrongdoing.

Penry Buckley

Icac hears more phone messages from fugitive property developer

Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet does not have much longer in the witness box at Icac today. The inquiry has heard more intercepted phone calls from fugitive property developer Jean Nassif for the first time since the opening day of the inquiry.

The corruption watchdog is examining a second allegation that between 2020 and 2023, Nassif and his company Toplace made prohibited donations solicited or accepted by Christian Ellis, Jeremy Greenwood and Charles Perrottet in exchange for the pursuit of outcomes sought by Nassif, including damage to the career of former Liberal Baulkham Hills MP David Elliott, and the removal of the then-building commissioner David Chandler.

Elliott retired after his seat was abolished and he was unable to convince local branches in Castle Hill to make him the candidate.

But the inquiry has yet to focus extensively on the allegation. At the close of play, Jean-Claude Perrottet has been played three phone calls between him and Nassif in 2021, when he was managing shares for Nassif while working at Medallion Financial.

In one call, Nassif can be heard to ask Jean-Claude Perrottet to withdraw “100” from his portfolio to give to “to your brother, to Jeremy or Chris”.

Nassif says, “I was thinking to give it to your brother for pre-selection for now, and ... I’ll give you a million in a couple of weeks’ time,” but Jean-Claude Perrottet says “wow, that’d be great”, but tells him it is not possible to withdraw money from his portfolio.

Asked about which brother Nassif was proposing to give $100,000 for pre-selections, he says: “I don’t. I don’t know what he’s talking about, to be honest with you ... it makes no sense.” He rejects the suggestion that the money was to support the Reformers recruitment work. “I just don’t agree with that characterisation. This is obviously just nonsense.”

Asked about which brother Nassif was proposing to give money for pre-selections, he says:

I don’t. I don’t know what he’s talking about, to be honest with you ... it makes no sense.

He rejects the suggestion that the money was to support the Reformers recruitment work.

I just don’t agree with that characterisation. This is obviously just nonsense.

Caitlin Cassidy

ABC’s head of investigations leaves national broadcaster

The head of investigations and current affairs at the ABC, Jo Puccini, has resigned after more than two decades with the national broadcaster.

In an email to staff on Thursday afternoon, acting news director of the ABC, Donna Field, wished her “every success in whatever comes next”:

After more than 25 years, Head of Investigations and Current Affairs, Jo Puccini is leaving the ABC. Jo’s journalistic contribution includes her early award-winning work at Four Corners and senior roles at Media Watch, Lateline, 7.30, the National Reporting Team and ABC Investigations. Jo has helped shape significant public interest journalism and built high-performing teams, leading to numerous Walkley awards.

A statement attributed to Puccini in the all-staff email said she was “proud of the journalism” she’d helped produce, describing her time there as an “adventure and a privilege”.

It’s now time for a new chapter in my career. I’ll be watching and cheering you all on to great success and important journalism that will continue to benefit the Australian public.

Puccini had faced backlash for overseeing the former-bikie turned journalist, Mahmood Fazal, during his time at Four Corners. An investigation into the veracity of sources used on two programs hosted by Fazal, that aired in 2023 and 2024, are ongoing. Guardian Australia is not suggesting this was why she left the ABC.

Luca Ittimani

Realestate.com.au sees ‘early days’ of housing market recovery

The head of realestate.com.au has called out early signs the housing market could be stabilising, with new listings falling and home buyers still watching the market.

Cam McIntyre, REA Group’s chief executive, told shareholders that the website had recorded rising homebuyer interest, in a call announcing the company’s financial results. McIntyre said:

Customers are starting to settle, and they are coming back to loan applications, and we are gradually seeing improvements in application volume. I’d say a little bit early days, but we have definitely seen improvement there over recent weeks.

McIntyre reported high web traffic, suggesting hopeful buyers were engaged, while new listings were falling in Melbourne and Sydney, the two cities that have led the price falls. Indicators of future seller interest were flat or falling, he said.

House prices are falling in part because fewer people are interested in buying but more are selling. Reversal of those trends would limit the extent of price falls.

Ray White, the real estate agency, has reported rising numbers of investors and active bidders at its auctions.

Cotality, the property data company, has reported new listings have fallen to levels seen in July 2025 as sellers adjust to meet the market. Melbourne’s auction clearance rate last week rose to a 12-week high of 54.7%, though the national rate fell to 48.9%, as conditions vary across the country.

Icac witness asked about ‘filthy schools money’ messages

Penry Buckley

Returning to the NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny, Jean-Claude Perrottet has been asked about messages read out on the first day of the inquiry.

On 12 January 2023, Reformer Jeremy Greenwood allegedly wrote to him:

Hey, so you know how I’m good to you and help you and give you all your filthy schools money … and put up with your fucking whining?

Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote back: “Don’t put that in writing.”

Greenwood replied: “It deletes.”

Counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asks if the messages are “because it wasn’t money that you or he were being paid for any work that you were doing for Catholic Schools NSW?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “No, I think Jeremy was doing work for Catholic Schools.”

Curtin: “Why is he, why is he calling it filthy schools money?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “I can’t speak to his thoughts, but he’s having a crack at me.”

Curtin: “OK, well then, if it was just a joke and he’s having a crack, why do you then respond quickly: ‘Don’t put that in writing’?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Why would I want that in writing?”

Curtin: “Why wouldn’t you?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Because it’s not true.”

Evacuation declared after industrial shed fire creates toxic smoke in Port Adelaide

Locals have been urged to evacuate immediately after a fire in Port Adelaide at an industrial shed used to store sulphur began producing large volumes of toxic smoke.

South Australia’s Metropolitan Fire Service has said anyone within 1km of Moonta Road in Port Adelaide should leave immediately and others should not enter the area.

A warning from the fire service said:

It is extremely dangerous.

Emergency services are on the scene, the smoke is considered toxic.

The fire is contained to the shed, and heavy smoke is blowing in a south-easterly direction, according to the latest update.

However, the wind direction could change and anyone in the vicinity has been advised to close their windows and doors and be cautious of smoke.

The SA Ambulance Service said two people have been taken to the Royal Adelaide hospital.

Albanese to welcome president of Vietnam next week

Prime minister Anthony Albanese will welcome the general secretary and president of Vietnam, To Lam, to Australia next week.

The leaders will meet in Canberra on Tuesday, 11 August to “discuss opportunities to deepen cooperation” as part of the Vietnamese leader’s first visit to Australia.

The prime minister said in a statement:

I look forward to welcoming General Secretary and President To Lam to Australia and discussing how we can strengthen cooperation between our two nations.

The Vietnam-Australia relationship is grounded in deep strategic trust, mutual interests, and a shared ambition for the future of our region.

Our two nations share deep cultural ties and around 350,000 Australians have Vietnamese heritage.

Penry Buckley

The inquiry has previously heard evidence that Beckington, set up by Reformers Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood in 2019, received payments from prohibited donor, hotelier Michael O’Hara, for factional work, after issuing fake invoices for consulting advice.

O’Hara admitted to the arrangement last week, but disputed whether the payments counted as political donations.

Curtin says Ellis wrote to Jean-Claude Perrottet: “O’Hara pays GST, but it’s included in the five”. She puts it to him that the money O’Hara was paying to Beckington was being used to pay him. “I honestly don’t recall whether that’s the case,” he says.

Penry Buckley

‘You sneaky man’: messages suggest Reformers quibbled over GST on $5,000 payments, inquiry hears

The NSW Icac’s Operation Rosny has resumed after lunch. Questions have returned to $5,000 payments received by Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet from lobbying company Beckington, controlled by fellow Reformer Christian Ellis.

Earlier the inquiry heard he received an initial monthly payment of $5,500, followed by four monthly payments of $5,000, between April and August 2021, but he said he could not recall doing any work for Beckington.

This afternoon, he has been read messages between him and Ellis, in which he wrote to Ellis: “Any chance you can send the money today?”, to which Ellis responds, “What money?”. After Jean-Claude Perrottet writes “please”, Ellis responds: “All right. But it’s 5k, not five and a half, you sneaky man”.

Counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin suggests that this indicates confusion between Ellis and Jean-Claude Perrottet about how to manage the GST in invoices. She reads further messages discussing GST in which Ellis calls Jean-Claude Perrottet a “slippery man”. Jean-Claude writes: “Yeah, I’m easy, I just thought I had to include it.” Ellis calls him a “slippery man” again, to which Perrottet writes back: “Haha, get out”.

‘Angus Taylor hates Rob’: federal opposition leader referenced at Icac again

Penry Buckley

Returning to the NSW Icac, federal opposition leader Angus Taylor’s name has been mentioned again during hearings, raising the question of if he ever has donated to the Reformers.

Taylor, who is not named in Icac’s allegations, has previously denied ever making payments to the group.

Jean-Claude Perrottet has been read text messages sent by Reformer Christian Ellis to him in September 2021, in which Ellis says the group has “zero dollars at the moment”. Asked why by Jean Claude-Perrottet, Ellis writes:

“Because Michael O’Hara hates the vax campaign, and Angus Taylor hates Rob”.

The inquiry has previously heard evidence, including from Reformer Robert Assaf, that hotelier Michael O’Hara threatened to end an arrangement in which he paid lobbying company Beckington for Reformers factional work, after the group adopted an anti-vaccination stance.

Counsel assisting, Juliet Curtin, asks: “That seems to be suggesting that Mr Taylor had paid some money for the Reformers too, doesn’t it, or was refusing to?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “It sounds like that’s the suggestion.”

Curtin: “Do you know anything about that?”

Jean-Claude Perrottet: “Look, I’ve I’ve heard it come up [at the inquiry], but until that came up, I hadn’t recalled that at all.”

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Achol Arok will take the lead from here. Enjoy your Thursday.
